# Gauss-Newton (BHHH)

> **Maturity: beta** — see [Feature Maturity](../maturity.qmd) for what this means.

The Gauss-Newton optimizer is an alternative to the standard FOCE/FOCEI approach that exploits the nonlinear-least-squares structure of the FOCE objective. It uses the BHHH (Berndt-Hall-Hall-Hausman) approximation to the Hessian and typically converges in 10-30 iterations, compared to 100+ evaluations for gradient-based methods like SLSQP.

This approach mirrors NONMEM's modified Gauss-Newton algorithm.

## Variants

| Method | Key | Description |
|--------|-----|-------------|
| Pure Gauss-Newton | `gn` | Fast convergence for well-conditioned problems |
| GN + FOCEI hybrid | `gn_hybrid` | Runs GN first, then polishes with FOCEI for robustness |

## Algorithm Overview

### BHHH Hessian Approximation

The FOCE objective has the form:

$$
\text{OFV} = 2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} \text{NLL}_i
$$

The BHHH approximation uses the outer product of per-subject gradients as an approximate Hessian:

$$
H_{\text{BHHH}} = 4 \sum_{i=1}^{N} g_i \, g_i^T
$$

where $g_i = \nabla_x \text{NLL}_i$ is the gradient of the negative log-likelihood for subject $i$ with respect to the packed parameter vector, evaluated with each subject's EBEs $\hat\eta_i$ held fixed.

Per-subject gradients come from a closed form at fixed $\hat\eta_i$ whenever the model is inside its scope:

- **Almquist Laplace** when `interaction = true` (FOCEI): the exact fixed-EBE score in $\Omega$ and $\sigma$, with the $\theta$ axis contracted exactly from the fixed-$\eta$ θ-adjoint (one reverse sweep per eight weight rows). Runs on analytical and ODE models and on per-compartment error models.
- **Sheiner–Beal** when `interaction = false` (FOCE): the same $\theta$ axis, but its linearisation additionally requires an analytical (non-ODE) structural model and a single error model.

Where a closed form does not apply, the score is the **exact fixed-EBE score of the analytic likelihood kernel** — the per-subject objective with $\hat\eta_i$ and $H$ held, one reverse sweep plus the θ contractions. That covers what the closed forms decline: M3 BLOQ censoring, inter-occasion variability (the stacked marginal at $[\hat\eta, \hat\kappa]$), IIV on the residual error, a θ-dependent residual-error magnitude, `block_sigma` residual correlations, FREM rows, and a non-Gaussian data term (`[event_model]` TTE / RTTE, `[binary_model]`, CTMM — over the BSV block under IOV). The closed forms' own scope is `closed_form_fixed_ebe_grad_ok` in [`src/estimation/gauss_newton.rs`](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/blob/main/src/estimation/gauss_newton.rs), whose doc comment says, for each exclusion, which term of the objective they do not carry.

Central finite differences of the per-subject objective remain only for an endpoint without an exact channel and for a subject outside the recorders' scope (see [Known FD fallbacks](foce.qmd#known-fd-fallbacks)). A closed form also hands one subject on to the kernel score at one evaluation when the matrix it factorises ($\tilde H$ for Laplace, $\tilde R$ for Sheiner–Beal) is not positive definite.

These are the scores the BHHH matrix is built from. They are **not** the gradient GN steps
along on a FOCEI model. The Laplace marginal carries $\log|\tilde H(\hat\eta_i)|$, and holding
$\hat\eta_i$ fixed drops its response $\partial_\eta \log|\tilde H| \cdot d\hat\eta_i/dx$, which is
non-zero under proportional or combined error. So for every FOCEI subject with random effects,
GN steps along the subject's exact total derivative: the analytic adjoint at the mode, or a
finite difference with $\hat\eta_i$ re-solved at each point where the adjoint declines. The
same holds for a TTE or discrete endpoint under FOCE. Before
[#2740](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2740), the gradient was the score plus a
θ-only approximation of that term, or nothing at all past the closed forms (M3, IIV on RUV, …).
It disagreed with the objective, sometimes in sign, and GN's trust region collapsed far from
the optimum (`warfarin_bloq` stopped 10.6 OFV above FOCEI). FOCE Gaussian models keep the
fixed-EBE score.

On a subject with IOV, the gradient GN steps along is not the fixed-EBE score either: it is the
per-subject outer gradient the NLopt optimizers take, with $\hat\eta_i$ and the occasion
$\hat\kappa_{ik}$ responding to $x$. That gradient is exact where the analytic adjoint serves
the subject, and a reconverged finite difference otherwise. Without it, `method = gn` stopped
on `examples/warfarin_iov.ferx` near its initial estimates, 22.9 OFV above the optimum, while
reporting convergence ([#2455](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2455)). The BHHH
matrix stays on the raw score $g_i$.

This approximation is equivalent to the Gauss-Newton Hessian for log-likelihood objectives and is guaranteed positive semi-definite.

### Trust region

Each iteration takes one trust-region step on the quadratic model built from the gradient and
$H_{\text{BHHH}}$. Before the solve, every coordinate is divided by a per-parameter scale (fixed
from the initial estimates; identity with `scale_params = false`) so the system is better
conditioned. The radius is measured in this scaled space.

- **The step:** $\delta$ approximately minimises $g^T\delta + \tfrac12\,\delta^T H_{\text{BHHH}}\,\delta$
  subject to $\lVert\delta\rVert \le \Delta$, by Steihaug truncated conjugate gradients. CG stops
  once its residual is small, steps to the boundary when it would leave the region or meets a
  direction of non-positive curvature, and runs at most
  $\max(\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil, 5)$ iterations for $n$ packed parameters.
  There is no damping factor, Cholesky solve or line search.
- **The trial point:** the inner loop re-estimates every subject's EBEs at $x + \delta$
  (warm-started from the current EBEs), so the trial OFV is the FOCE/FOCEI objective, not the
  quadratic model.
- **The ratio:** $\rho$ is the actual OFV reduction divided by the reduction the quadratic model
  predicts. A non-finite trial OFV counts as $\rho < 0$, and so does a step clamped at a bound
  whose predicted reduction is no longer positive.
- **The radius:** $\Delta$ starts at 1 and never exceeds 10.

| $\rho$ | Step | Radius |
|--------|------|--------|
| $< 0.25$ | rejected | $\Delta / 4$ |
| $0.25$ to $0.75$ | accepted | unchanged |
| $> 0.75$ | accepted | $\min(2\Delta,\ 10)$ |

A rejected step costs an iteration but keeps the current estimates. When the quadratic model
predicts almost no reduction ($< 10^{-10}$) while the gradient is not zero, the BHHH matrix is
degenerate along the step: the radius is divided by 4 and the next iteration starts, with no
trial point evaluated. That iteration still counts toward `maxiter`.

### Bounds and stalled steps

A parameter that reaches its bound while the gradient still pushes it outward is held for that
iteration, the way a `FIX` parameter is, and the rest of the step is solved without it. When a
step does run into a bound, the trust region judges it against the reduction the quadratic model
predicts for the step actually taken, not the unclamped one. Before
[#2777](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2777) the clamped coordinate still claimed
its share of the prediction, so the ratio of actual to predicted reduction stayed at a fixed
value below 0.25 at every radius and the fit stopped on "trust radius collapsed"
(`examples/one_cpt_transit.ferx` under `method = gn`: 1513.94; now 1492.17, with `TVV` on its
upper bound of 500 and no collapse).

After three rejected steps in a row that no bound clamped, GN checks whether one subject's
EBE-response term sets the step direction: its term is at least 10 times every other subject's,
and on some parameter it outweighs the rest of the gradient. That happens when the subject's EBE
mode moves sharply with the parameters (for example near a fold), so its slope is exact at the
point but wrong over any step GN can take. GN then uses that subject's raw score for the rest of
the fit and adds a warning that names it. The reported final gradient keeps the subject's full
term.

### Convergence

The GN loop ends at the first of:

- **Converged, small change:** an accepted step changes the OFV by less than $10^{-6}$ relative
  to $\max(\lvert\text{OFV}\rvert, 1)$, from iteration 4 on, and the trust radius the step
  was taken at is at least $10^{-3}$. One such step is enough. Below that radius a step changes
  the OFV little *because* it is tiny, whatever the gradient, so it does not count; the loop goes
  on and ends on one of the rules below
  ([#2738](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2738)). Near a real optimum the
  quadratic model predicts well, so accepted steps double the radius and it climbs back above
  $10^{-3}$ within a few iterations.
- **Converged, stationary point:** the predicted reduction is below $10^{-10}$ and the scaled
  gradient norm is below $10^{-8}$.
- **Not converged, trust radius collapsed:** the radius falls below $10^{-10}$, after rejected
  steps or degenerate-BHHH retries. The fit adds the warning "Gauss-Newton: trust radius
  collapsed without convergence" (or "degenerate BHHH Hessian, trust radius collapsed without
  convergence"), classified critical, like the budget warning.
- **Not converged, budget spent:** `maxiter` iterations ran, with the warning "Gauss-Newton:
  max iterations reached without convergence". Only this stop carries it: a collapsed radius or
  a cancelled fit reports its own reason alone
  ([#1049](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1049)).

This is the loop's verdict, not yet the fit's. Pure `gn` re-checks `converged` afterwards: a
cold re-solve of the EBEs at the final estimates
([#2097](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2097)), the covariance step's check that
the end point is stationary ([#2785](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2785)), and a
check that the final objective is finite can each demote it.

The optimizer trace (`optimizer_trace = true`) logs one row per step. For GN rows its
`lm_lambda` column holds the trust radius: the radius the step was tried with on a rejected row,
and the radius after the update on an accepted one. The column keeps its old name, from the
Levenberg-Marquardt loop GN ran before 0.1.0, so existing readers still find it.

## Hybrid Mode (GN + FOCEI)

When `method = gn_hybrid`, the algorithm runs in two phases:

1. **GN phase**: Run Gauss-Newton iterations to quickly find the basin of the minimum
2. **FOCEI polish**: Run up to 100 iterations of standard FOCEI optimization, warm-started from the GN result. The polish stage uses the configured outer optimizer (`optimizer` in `[fit_options]`), which defaults to `auto`: `nlopt_lbfgs` when the exact analytic gradient is available (e.g. warfarin), `bobyqa` otherwise — see [Outer Optimizers](optimizers.qmd#the-auto-default) for the full rule.

The final result is whichever phase produced the lower OFV. This combines the fast convergence of Gauss-Newton with the refined accuracy of FOCEI.

## Configuration

```
[fit_options]
  method     = gn          # or gn_hybrid
  maxiter    = 100         # max GN iterations
  covariance = true
```

The trust region has no user setting: the starting radius, its cap and the CG budget are fixed
as described under [Trust region](#trust-region). `gn_lambda`, the Levenberg-Marquardt damping
factor of the loop GN replaced in 0.1.0, has no effect. ferx still accepts the key but warns when
it is set, on any method, and the next minor release removes it.

## When to Use

**Use `gn`** when:
- You want fast convergence and the model is well-conditioned
- You are iterating on model development and need quick feedback

**Use `gn_hybrid`** when:
- You want robustness against local minima
- The model is complex (many parameters or random effects)
- You want the speed of GN with a safety net

**Stick with `foce`/`focei`** when:
- The model has convergence issues with GN (rare)
- You need exact compatibility with standard FOCE/FOCEI results
- The model has **no random effects** and you are not confident in the `sigma`
  start (see below)

### Fixed-effects-only models

`gn` and `gn_hybrid` both reduce correctly at `n_eta = 0`
([no omega at all](../model-file/parameters.qmd#no-omega-at-all-fixed-effects-only-naive-pooled-fits)),
but GN is the method most sensitive to the starting values there. Without random
effects there is no inner EBE loop to absorb a mis-specified `sigma`, so the
initial objective can start orders of magnitude above the optimum, and BHHH's
outer-product Hessian badly over-estimates curvature that far out — the step
collapses and the fit crawls into `maxiter`.

Concretely, on `examples/one_cpt_iv_pooled.ferx` and its own
`sigma PROP_ERR ~ 0.02 (sd)` start, `gn` begins at OFV 11374, stops at **8670**
and reports `Converged: NO` with ~6900% RSEs, where `foce`, `focei`, `laplace`
and `gn_hybrid` all reach **−269.6370**. That is a wrong answer, not an imprecise
one, so `gn` is **not recommended** for fixed-effects-only models. From
`0.13 (sd)` it does converge, to −269.6322 — the right basin, still 0.005 short of
FOCEI's −269.6370. FOCEI reaches the optimum from either start. If a
fixed-effects GN fit stalls, check `sigma` before anything else — or use
`gn_hybrid`, whose FOCEI polish recovers it.

Since [#1006](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1006) the combination
is flagged rather than left to the reader: `ferx check` emits
`W_GN_NO_RANDOM_EFFECTS` for `method = gn` at `n_eta = 0`, and a pure-GN run that
ends `Converged: NO` there adds a post-fit warning saying the result may be badly
wrong rather than merely imprecise — `Converged: NO` is the state that actually
predicts the bad answer. `gn_hybrid` is exempt from both, since its FOCEI polish
recovers the optimum — and so is a hand-written `method = [gn, focei]`, which is
the same polish spelled out. The rule is "`gn` is the last estimating stage": a
GN result something else re-optimises is not the result you get.

The two split the message between them: `W_GN_NO_RANDOM_EFFECTS` carries the
remedy (prefer `gn_hybrid` or `focei`, or improve the `sigma` start), the post-fit
warning carries only the outcome. A run that trips both — the usual case for a
standalone `gn` — therefore states the advice once, not twice.
